title: How RAG systems retrieve, rank, and cite evidence
description: A practical quiz on how RAG systems chunk, retrieve, rank, cite, and evaluate information, and where they break. Each explanation links to a paper or technical doc.

questions.title: What two kinds of memory did the original RAG model combine?

images.alt: One RAG request drawn as two rows of stages. The offline ingestion row runs source docs through chunking, passage embedding, and indexing. The index is labelled non-parametric memory, with a note that a source edit that never reaches the index is an ingestion bug. In the query-time row, the user query goes to two parallel branches: dense approximate nearest neighbours over stored vectors, and lexical BM25 for exact codes, names, and ids. They merge in an RRF fuse box computing 1 / (60 + rank), then a cross-encoder reranks the top n, and the result goes into a prompt, a generator labelled parametric memory, and an answer with citations. A footer names the metric for each stage, and a closing strip reads: a reranker only reorders the candidates it was handed.
images.caption: Lewis et al. call the sequence-to-sequence model parametric memory and the dense Wikipedia index non-parametric memory.

options.text: A pretrained sequence-to-sequence model and a dense Wikipedia index searched by a neural retriever
Two independently prompted generators whose answers were decided by majority vote
A keyword index and a rules engine, with no learned generator
A larger context window and a lower sampling temperature, with no external memory

questions.explanation: Lewis et al. call the sequence-to-sequence model parametric memory and the dense Wikipedia index non-parametric memory. A neural retriever searches the index, and the generator reads the passages it returns. A bigger context window or different decoding settings don't turn a model into RAG.
questions.references: [Lewis et al.: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)

images.caption: The model pulls passages from a dense index and hands them to the generator. Because the index is non-parametric memory, the generator's weights don't have to store the source corpus.

options.text: The generator conditions on passages fetched from an external index.
The external index is non-parametric memory.
All source documents must be memorized in the generator's weights before inference.
Adding retrieval makes every generated claim factually correct.

questions.explanation: The model pulls passages from a dense index and hands them to the generator. Because the index is non-parametric memory, the generator's weights don't have to store the source corpus. Retrieval still doesn't guarantee a correct answer. RAGTruth documents RAG outputs with unsupported and contradictory claims.

questions.title: A chunk splits a refund rule from its exception. What should you fix first?
questions.description: The policy says: "Refunds are allowed within 30 days, unless the license key has been activated." Retrieval returns only the part that allows refunds.

images.alt: Three panels about chunking. The first splits "Refunds are allowed within 30 days, unless the license key has been activated." at a character count. A highlighted chunk holds only the permissive clause, and a greyed chunk holds the exception. A fixed version keeps both in one self-contained unit. The second panel lays out four retrieval units: whole document, section, passage, and proposition. It notes that one unit means one vector. The third draws three overlapping fixed windows with the shared regions framed. Overlap puts a boundary fact in both neighbours, but the same text is indexed twice, so results can be near-duplicates. A note says overlap finds no semantic boundaries and changes no embedding dimension.
images.caption: The retrieved chunk no longer holds the full rule, so fix the chunking before tuning the generator. The Dense X Retrieval study found that the choice of retrieval unit affects both retrieval and downstream QA.

options.text: Change the chunking so the rule and its exception stay in one self-contained unit, then retest retrieval.
Keep the chunks and raise the generation temperature.
Keep the chunks and increase the embedding dimension.
Retrieve more unrelated policy chunks for extra context.

questions.explanation: The retrieved chunk no longer holds the full rule, so fix the chunking before tuning the generator. The Dense X Retrieval study found that the choice of retrieval unit affects both retrieval and downstream QA. Its units are propositions, which are short, self-contained facts. Here, the rule and its exception belong in the same unit.
questions.references: [Chen et al.: Dense X Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06648)

questions.title: Why can whole-document chunks work poorly for clause-level questions?

images.alt: Three panels about chunking. The first splits "Refunds are allowed within 30 days, unless the license key has been activated." at a character count. A highlighted chunk holds only the permissive clause, and a greyed chunk holds the exception. A fixed version keeps both in one self-contained unit. The second panel lays out four retrieval units: whole document, section, passage, and proposition. It notes that one unit means one vector. The third draws three overlapping fixed windows with the shared regions framed. Overlap puts a boundary fact in both neighbours, but the same text is indexed twice, so results can be near-duplicates. A note says overlap finds no semantic boundaries and changes no embedding dimension.
images.caption: A whole manual can cover many unrelated topics, so a single embedding may be too broad for a narrow query.

options.text: One vector has to represent many topics, which can make a narrow clause harder to match.
Embedding APIs accept sentences but reject documents by definition.
Whole documents cannot be assigned source metadata.
Dense retrieval works only when every indexed unit has exactly one sentence.

questions.explanation: A whole manual can cover many unrelated topics, so a single embedding may be too broad for a narrow query. Chen et al. compared documents, passages, sentences, and propositions as retrieval units, and the choice changed both retrieval and downstream results. That's a reason to test smaller self-contained units. It doesn't make one-sentence chunks a universal rule.
questions.references: [Chen et al.: Dense X Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06648)

questions.title: What can overlap between fixed-size chunks change?

images.alt: Three panels about chunking. The first splits "Refunds are allowed within 30 days, unless the license key has been activated." at a character count. A highlighted chunk holds only the permissive clause, and a greyed chunk holds the exception. A fixed version keeps both in one self-contained unit. The second panel lays out four retrieval units: whole document, section, passage, and proposition. It notes that one unit means one vector. The third draws three overlapping fixed windows with the shared regions framed. Overlap puts a boundary fact in both neighbours, but the same text is indexed twice, so results can be near-duplicates. A note says overlap finds no semantic boundaries and changes no embedding dimension.
images.caption: With overlap, each chunk starts with text copied from the end of the previous one. That keeps context around a boundary, but it repeats text in the index and sometimes in the prompt.

options.text: A fact near a boundary can appear in both neighboring chunks.
The index holds repeated text, and retrieval can return near-duplicate chunks.
Every chunk ends on a semantic boundary.
The embedding model's vector dimension changes.

questions.explanation: With overlap, each chunk starts with text copied from the end of the previous one. That keeps context around a boundary, but it repeats text in the index and sometimes in the prompt. Overlap doesn't find semantic boundaries, and it doesn't change the embedding model's output dimension.
questions.references: [Microsoft Learn: Text Split skill](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/cognitive-search-skill-textsplit) · [Chen et al.: Dense X Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06648) · [Google AI for Developers: Understand and count tokens](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens)

questions.title: Why are dual encoders useful for first-stage retrieval over a large corpus?

images.alt: One RAG request drawn as two rows of stages. The offline ingestion row runs source docs through chunking, passage embedding, and indexing. The index is labelled non-parametric memory, with a note that a source edit that never reaches the index is an ingestion bug. In the query-time row, the user query goes to two parallel branches: dense approximate nearest neighbours over stored vectors, and lexical BM25 for exact codes, names, and ids. They merge in an RRF fuse box computing 1 / (60 + rank), then a cross-encoder reranks the top n, and the result goes into a prompt, a generator labelled parametric memory, and an answer with citations. A footer names the metric for each stage, and a closing strip reads: a reranker only reorders the candidates it was handed.
images.caption: DPR uses separate encoders for queries and passages. It can encode the corpus before any query arrives and store the vectors in an index.

options.text: You can encode documents ahead of time, then encode only the query at request time and compare it with the stored vectors.
It jointly processes every query-document pair before any document can be indexed.
It proves that the nearest document contains a factually correct answer.
It removes the need for an index by storing the corpus in the query vector.

questions.explanation: DPR uses separate encoders for queries and passages. It can encode the corpus before any query arrives and store the vectors in an index. At request time, it encodes only the query and searches those vectors. A model that scores each query-document pair jointly fits the smaller reranking stage better.
questions.references: [Karpukhin et al.: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906) · [Reimers and Gurevych: Sentence-BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084)

questions.title: For L2-normalized vectors, which score gives the same ranking as cosine similarity?

options.text: Dot product
Vector dimensionality
The sum of the vector's coordinates
Document token count

questions.explanation: Cosine similarity is `x·y / (||x|| ||y||)`. L2 normalization sets both norms to `1`, which leaves `x·y`. So for normalized vectors, dot product and cosine similarity give the same scores and the same ranking.
questions.references: [scikit-learn: cosine_similarity](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.pairwise.cosine_similarity.html)

questions.title: Dense retrieval misses an exact error code. What should you add?
questions.description: Dense search finds related troubleshooting pages but misses the runbook with the exact code.

images.alt: One RAG request drawn as two rows of stages. The offline ingestion row runs source docs through chunking, passage embedding, and indexing. The index is labelled non-parametric memory, with a note that a source edit that never reaches the index is an ingestion bug. In the query-time row, the user query goes to two parallel branches: dense approximate nearest neighbours over stored vectors, and lexical BM25 for exact codes, names, and ids. They merge in an RRF fuse box computing 1 / (60 + rank), then a cross-encoder reranks the top n, and the result goes into a prompt, a generator labelled parametric memory, and an answer with citations. A footer names the metric for each stage, and a closing strip reads: a reranker only reorders the candidates it was handed.
images.caption: Vector search is good at matching meaning, and keyword search is good at matching exact strings. The Azure AI Search docs list product codes, names, dates, and specialized terms as cases where keyword search can do better.

options.text: Add a lexical retrieval branch and fuse its results with the vector results.
Remove the error code from the query before embedding it.
Raise the generation temperature until the model guesses the right runbook.
Replace every identifier in the corpus with a generic word such as `error`.

questions.explanation: Vector search is good at matching meaning, and keyword search is good at matching exact strings. The Azure AI Search docs list product codes, names, dates, and specialized terms as cases where keyword search can do better. A hybrid query runs both and merges their rankings.
questions.references: [Microsoft Learn: Hybrid Search in Azure AI Search](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/hybrid-search-overview)

questions.title: What can go wrong with approximate nearest-neighbor search?

options.text: It's fast, but it can miss the exact nearest neighbor for some queries.
It converts the stored embeddings back into approximate source sentences.
Every returned document has about the same relevance.
Similarity scores become the probability that a passage is factually correct.

questions.explanation: HNSW searches a layered proximity graph instead of comparing the query with every vector. That makes search fast, but an approximate method can miss the exact nearest neighbor. Similarity measures how close two vectors are, not how likely a passage is to be correct.
questions.references: [Malkov and Yashunin: Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using HNSW](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320)

questions.title: Three of four relevant chunks appear in the top five results. What is recall@5?

images.alt: Three panels on ranking. The first shows a BM25 result list scored 18.4 down to 6.2 beside a dense vector list scored 0.83 down to 0.71, then the reciprocal rank fusion of doc-A: 1 / (60 + 4) + 1 / (60 + 1) = 0.01563 + 0.01639 = 0.03202. A note says ranks are comparable by construction, so no normalization is needed. The second shows five result slots, three marked relevant and two not, plus a fourth relevant chunk stranded at rank 23, with the arithmetic recall@5 = 3 relevant found / 4 relevant total = 0.75. The third lists what raising k from 5 to 50 trades: recall can rise, distractors arrive, and context is spent.
images.caption: Recall is the number of relevant items retrieved divided by the total number of relevant items.

questions.explanation: Recall is the number of relevant items retrieved divided by the total number of relevant items. Here that's `3 / 4 = 0.75`. The two irrelevant results lower precision, not recall.
questions.references: [NIST TREC: Evaluation of Ranked Lists](https://trec.nist.gov/presentations/TREC9/overview/tsld014.htm)

questions.title: Why might raising retrieval `k` from 5 to 50 make the answer worse?
questions.description: The system sends every retrieved passage to the generator.

images.alt: Three panels on ranking. The first shows a BM25 result list scored 18.4 down to 6.2 beside a dense vector list scored 0.83 down to 0.71, then the reciprocal rank fusion of doc-A: 1 / (60 + 4) + 1 / (60 + 1) = 0.01563 + 0.01639 = 0.03202. A note says ranks are comparable by construction, so no normalization is needed. The second shows five result slots, three marked relevant and two not, plus a fourth relevant chunk stranded at rank 23, with the arithmetic recall@5 = 3 relevant found / 4 relevant total = 0.75. The third lists what raising k from 5 to 50 trades: recall can rise, distractors arrive, and context is spent.
images.caption: Raising `k` can recover more relevant chunks, but it also lets in lower-ranked distractors.

images.alt: Two panels. The first shows an 8,192-token combined budget as one bar: 2,100 tokens of instructions and query, five retrieved chunks of 900 each, a 1,200-token answer reserve, and a thin sliver labelled 392 tokens left. The arithmetic reads 2,100 + (5 × 900) + 1,200 = 7,800 and 8,192 − 7,800 = 392. The second plots the Lost in the Middle curve: accuracy against the position of the relevant passage among twenty, high at the first and last positions and lowest in the middle. Beside it, the same five chunks sit in prompt order, with the first and last marked read reliably and the third marked buried. A closing strip reads: fitting inside the window is a capacity fact, not a promise that every detail is used.
images.caption: The context window is finite, so every extra chunk leaves fewer tokens for instructions and the answer.

options.text: Recall may go up, but the extra passages can distract the generator and use up context.
A generator is mathematically unable to read more than five retrieved passages.
Recall always drops when `k` increases.
Every vector index returns exactly the same documents for every value of `k`.

questions.explanation: More passages can bring more supporting evidence, but they can also bring hard distractors and use up prompt tokens. Amiraz et al. report cases where irrelevant retrieved passages led the model to answer incorrectly. Test `k` against both retrieval and end-to-end metrics instead of assuming more passages always help.
questions.references: [Amiraz et al.: The Distracting Effect](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.892/) · [Google AI for Developers: Understand and count tokens](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens)

questions.title: With a rank constant of 60, what RRF score do ranks 1 and 4 produce?
questions.description: Use `score = 1 / (60 + rank1) + 1 / (60 + rank2)`. Enter a decimal rounded to five places.

images.alt: Three panels on ranking. The first shows a BM25 result list scored 18.4 down to 6.2 beside a dense vector list scored 0.83 down to 0.71, then the reciprocal rank fusion of doc-A: 1 / (60 + 4) + 1 / (60 + 1) = 0.01563 + 0.01639 = 0.03202. A note says ranks are comparable by construction, so no normalization is needed. The second shows five result slots, three marked relevant and two not, plus a fourth relevant chunk stranded at rank 23, with the arithmetic recall@5 = 3 relevant found / 4 relevant total = 0.75. The third lists what raising k from 5 to 50 trades: recall can rise, distractors arrive, and context is spent.
images.caption: Plug the ranks into the formula: `1/61 + 1/64 = 0.01639344 + 0.015625 = 0.03201844`.

questions.explanation: Plug the ranks into the formula: `1/61 + 1/64 = 0.01639344 + 0.015625 = 0.03201844`. Rounded to five decimal places, that's `0.03202`. RRF adds one reciprocal term for each result list that contains the document.
questions.references: [Elasticsearch Reference: Reciprocal Rank Fusion](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/reciprocal-rank-fusion)

questions.title: Why can RRF combine BM25 and vector rankings without normalizing their raw scores?

images.alt: Three panels on ranking. The first shows a BM25 result list scored 18.4 down to 6.2 beside a dense vector list scored 0.83 down to 0.71, then the reciprocal rank fusion of doc-A: 1 / (60 + 4) + 1 / (60 + 1) = 0.01563 + 0.01639 = 0.03202. A note says ranks are comparable by construction, so no normalization is needed. The second shows five result slots, three marked relevant and two not, plus a fourth relevant chunk stranded at rank 23, with the arithmetic recall@5 = 3 relevant found / 4 relevant total = 0.75. The third lists what raising k from 5 to 50 trades: recall can rise, distractors arrive, and context is spent.
images.caption: BM25 and vector search produce scores on different scales with different meanings. RRF never compares those raw scores.

options.text: It works with each document's rank in each result list, so it never compares the raw scores.
It converts every raw score into a calibrated probability of truth.
It discards documents that appear in more than one result list.
It requires BM25 and vector search to use the same scoring equation.

questions.explanation: BM25 and vector search produce scores on different scales with different meanings. RRF never compares those raw scores. For each result list, it adds `1 / (k + rank)` for the document, so a document that ranks well in one or more lists gets a higher fused score.
questions.references: [Elasticsearch Reference: Reciprocal Rank Fusion](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/reciprocal-rank-fusion) · [Cormack, Clarke, and Büttcher: Reciprocal Rank Fusion](https://cormack.uwaterloo.ca/cormacksigir09-rrf.pdf)

questions.title: Where should an expensive query-passage reranker run?

images.alt: One RAG request drawn as two rows of stages. The offline ingestion row runs source docs through chunking, passage embedding, and indexing. The index is labelled non-parametric memory, with a note that a source edit that never reaches the index is an ingestion bug. In the query-time row, the user query goes to two parallel branches: dense approximate nearest neighbours over stored vectors, and lexical BM25 for exact codes, names, and ids. They merge in an RRF fuse box computing 1 / (60 + rank), then a cross-encoder reranks the top n, and the result goes into a prompt, a generator labelled parametric memory, and an answer with citations. A footer names the metric for each stage, and a closing strip reads: a reranker only reorders the candidates it was handed.
images.caption: A reranker reads the query and passage together, which costs more than comparing precomputed vectors.

options.text: After a fast retriever has narrowed the corpus to a smaller candidate set.
Against every document in the corpus for every query.
After generation, to reorder the words in the finished answer.
At ingestion time, using only document timestamps and no query.

questions.explanation: A reranker reads the query and passage together, which costs more than comparing precomputed vectors. So a typical pipeline first pulls a broad candidate set with a cheaper method, then reranks only that smaller set. Nogueira and Cho use BERT in this second-stage role.
questions.references: [Nogueira and Cho: Passage Re-ranking with BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04085) · [Reimers and Gurevych: Sentence-BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084)

questions.title: The retriever drops the only supporting passage. Can the reranker recover it?

images.alt: One RAG request drawn as two rows of stages. The offline ingestion row runs source docs through chunking, passage embedding, and indexing. The index is labelled non-parametric memory, with a note that a source edit that never reaches the index is an ingestion bug. In the query-time row, the user query goes to two parallel branches: dense approximate nearest neighbours over stored vectors, and lexical BM25 for exact codes, names, and ids. They merge in an RRF fuse box computing 1 / (60 + rank), then a cross-encoder reranks the top n, and the result goes into a prompt, a generator labelled parametric memory, and an answer with citations. A footer names the metric for each stage, and a closing strip reads: a reranker only reorders the candidates it was handed.
images.caption: Reranking changes the order of a candidate list. It doesn't add missing passages.

options.text: No. A reranker only scores the candidates it receives. Another retrieval step would have to add the missing passage.
Yes. A reranker reconstructs missing corpus passages from the query.
Yes. Every reranker searches the whole corpus before scoring.
No, because rerankers can process only irrelevant passages.

questions.explanation: Reranking changes the order of a candidate list. It doesn't add missing passages. If the retriever drops the only supporting passage, the reranker never sees it, so measure first-stage recall separately from reranking quality.
questions.references: [Nogueira and Cho: Passage Re-ranking with BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04085) · [NIST TREC: Evaluation of Ranked Lists](https://trec.nist.gov/presentations/TREC9/overview/tsld014.htm)

questions.title: What did the "Lost in the Middle" experiments find?

images.alt: Two panels. The first shows an 8,192-token combined budget as one bar: 2,100 tokens of instructions and query, five retrieved chunks of 900 each, a 1,200-token answer reserve, and a thin sliver labelled 392 tokens left. The arithmetic reads 2,100 + (5 × 900) + 1,200 = 7,800 and 8,192 − 7,800 = 392. The second plots the Lost in the Middle curve: accuracy against the position of the relevant passage among twenty, high at the first and last positions and lowest in the middle. Beside it, the same five chunks sit in prompt order, with the first and last marked read reliably and the third marked buried. A closing strip reads: fitting inside the window is a capacity fact, not a promise that every detail is used.
images.caption: Liu et al. moved the relevant information to different positions in multi-document QA and key-value retrieval tasks.

options.text: Models can use relevant information less reliably in the middle of the input than near the beginning or end, even when everything fits in the context window.
Models use information equally well at every position inside the context window.
Only retrieved information at the exact center can influence generation.
Long-context models cannot process more than one document.

questions.explanation: Liu et al. moved the relevant information to different positions in multi-document QA and key-value retrieval tasks. Performance was often better when the evidence came near the beginning or end, and worse when it sat in the middle. Fitting text into the context window doesn't mean the model uses every part equally well.
questions.references: [Liu et al.: Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)

questions.title: How many tokens are left in this context budget?
questions.description: The combined input and output limit is `8,192` tokens. Instructions and the query use `2,100`, five chunks use `900` each, and the answer reserves `1,200`. Enter the largest number of extra tokens that still fit.

images.alt: Two panels. The first shows an 8,192-token combined budget as one bar: 2,100 tokens of instructions and query, five retrieved chunks of 900 each, a 1,200-token answer reserve, and a thin sliver labelled 392 tokens left. The arithmetic reads 2,100 + (5 × 900) + 1,200 = 7,800 and 8,192 − 7,800 = 392. The second plots the Lost in the Middle curve: accuracy against the position of the relevant passage among twenty, high at the first and last positions and lowest in the middle. Beside it, the same five chunks sit in prompt order, with the first and last marked read reliably and the third marked buried. A closing strip reads: fitting inside the window is a capacity fact, not a promise that every detail is used.
images.caption: Five chunks use `5 × 900 = 4,500` tokens, so the total is `2,100 + 4,500 + 1,200 = 7,800`.

questions.explanation: Five chunks use `5 × 900 = 4,500` tokens, so the total is `2,100 + 4,500 + 1,200 = 7,800`. That leaves `8,192 - 7,800 = 392` tokens. Real limits vary by model, so check your model's documentation.
questions.references: [Google AI for Developers: Understand and count tokens](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens)

questions.title: What must a citation evaluator check?

options.text: Whether each citation actually supports the claim it's attached to
Whether every claim that needs evidence has a citation
Whether every cited page shares at least one keyword with the user's query, regardless of entailment
Whether the answer contains many links, even if none support its claims

questions.explanation: Citation correctness asks whether each citation supports its claim. Citation completeness asks whether every claim that needs evidence has a citation. An answer can fail either test by citing an irrelevant source, or by supporting one sentence and leaving other factual claims uncited. ALCE measures both. Link count and keyword overlap tell you neither.
questions.references: [Gao et al.: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14627)

questions.title: Why score provenance separately from answer accuracy?

options.text: A system can give a correct answer while retrieving or citing the wrong evidence, so answer quality alone doesn't show grounding.
Provenance is another name for generation latency.
Any correct answer proves that every retrieved passage was relevant.
Provenance matters only when the answer itself is false.

questions.explanation: A correct answer can still rest on the wrong evidence. The model might know the answer from its weights, or guess right while citing an irrelevant passage. KILT scores task performance and provenance separately, which exposes answers whose retrieval trail doesn't support them.
questions.references: [Petroni et al.: KILT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.02252)

questions.title: The right passage was retrieved. What can still go wrong?

options.text: The generator can add a claim that the retrieved passage doesn't support, or even contradicts.
The generator becomes physically unable to emit any token not copied from the passage.
The retrieval index automatically rewrites the source to match the answer.
Correct retrieval mathematically forces citation completeness to equal one.

questions.explanation: Retrieval supplies evidence, but the generator can still write claims the evidence doesn't support. RAGTruth documents RAG outputs with unsupported or contradictory claims. If the right passage was retrieved, the failure is in how the generator used it, not in retrieval recall.
questions.references: [Niu et al.: RAGTruth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.00396)

questions.title: Which parts of a RAG pipeline should you evaluate separately?

images.alt: One RAG request drawn as two rows of stages. The offline ingestion row runs source docs through chunking, passage embedding, and indexing. The index is labelled non-parametric memory, with a note that a source edit that never reaches the index is an ingestion bug. In the query-time row, the user query goes to two parallel branches: dense approximate nearest neighbours over stored vectors, and lexical BM25 for exact codes, names, and ids. They merge in an RRF fuse box computing 1 / (60 + rank), then a cross-encoder reranks the top n, and the result goes into a prompt, a generator labelled parametric memory, and an answer with citations. A footer names the metric for each stage, and a closing strip reads: a reranker only reorders the candidates it was handed.
images.caption: RAG has several stages, so a single end-to-end score can't show where a failure started. RAGAS scores the retrieved passages for relevance and focus, checks whether the answer stays faithful to them, and rates the answer itself.

options.text: Whether retrieval finds relevant, focused context
Whether generation stays faithful to the retrieved context
The quality of the answer itself
Only the visual appearance of the chat interface

questions.explanation: RAG has several stages, so a single end-to-end score can't show where a failure started. RAGAS scores the retrieved passages for relevance and focus, checks whether the answer stays faithful to them, and rates the answer itself. Separate scores tell you whether retrieval or generation went wrong.
questions.references: [Es et al.: RAGAS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15217)

questions.title: Why isn't one embedding leaderboard score enough to choose a model?

options.text: Embedding quality varies across tasks and domains, so you still need to test on your own retrieval workload.
Leaderboard models cannot produce numeric vectors.
A model that wins one benchmark is guaranteed to lose every other benchmark.
Retrieval benchmarks measure only generation temperature.

questions.explanation: MTEB covers several embedding tasks and found that no single method was best at all of them. BEIR tests retrieval across varied datasets, including out-of-distribution ones, where methods trade quality against cost differently. Use a leaderboard to shortlist models, then test them on queries, languages, documents, and relevance judgments from your own workload.
questions.references: [Muennighoff et al.: MTEB](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07316) · [Thakur et al.: BEIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663)

questions.title: Retrieval returns an outdated policy after the source changed. What should you fix?
questions.description: The source document was updated, but the old chunk and its embedding are still in the index.

images.alt: One RAG request drawn as two rows of stages. The offline ingestion row runs source docs through chunking, passage embedding, and indexing. The index is labelled non-parametric memory, with a note that a source edit that never reaches the index is an ingestion bug. In the query-time row, the user query goes to two parallel branches: dense approximate nearest neighbours over stored vectors, and lexical BM25 for exact codes, names, and ids. They merge in an RRF fuse box computing 1 / (60 + rank), then a cross-encoder reranks the top n, and the result goes into a prompt, a generator labelled parametric memory, and an answer with citations. A footer names the metric for each stage, and a closing strip reads: a reranker only reorders the candidates it was handed.
images.caption: The source changed, but the index didn't. Delete or replace the stale chunks and index the current document.

options.text: Fix ingestion: delete or replace the stale chunks, then index the current version.
Raise the generation temperature so the model invents a newer policy.
Keep both versions without timestamps and let the model pick one at random.
Retrain the generator and leave the stale index as it is.

questions.explanation: The source changed, but the index didn't. Delete or replace the stale chunks and index the current document. RAG keeps this knowledge outside the generator's weights, so the ingestion pipeline has to apply source updates and deletions. Generation settings can't make an old passage current.
questions.references: [Lewis et al.: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) · [Petroni et al.: KILT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.02252)

questions.title: Which RAG security risks have been demonstrated?

options.text: An attacker who can add malicious text to the knowledge base can steer answers to targeted queries.
Instructions hidden in retrieved websites or files can act as indirect prompt injection.
Using RAG removes prompt-injection risk entirely.
High vector similarity proves that retrieved content is safe to trust.

questions.explanation: PoisonedRAG shows that malicious text added to a knowledge base can steer answers to targeted questions. OWASP describes indirect prompt injection through external sources such as websites and files, and notes that RAG doesn't remove this risk. Similarity measures relevance, not trust, so treat retrieved content as untrusted input.
questions.references: [Zou et al.: PoisonedRAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07867) · [OWASP GenAI: Prompt Injection](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/)
